 ​5 questions to ask yourself before you say yes to marriage: Entrepreneur Ankur Warikoo reveals the real checklist​ 
 ​5 questions to ask yourself before you say yes to marriage: Entrepreneur Ankur Warikoo reveals the real checklist​ 
 TOI Lifestyle Desk / ETimes.in / Oct 13, 2026, 13:04 IST Save Share Aa + Text Size Small
 Medium
 Large
 1 / 7 5 questions to ask yourself before you say yes to marriage, Ankur Warikoo shares his checklist
 Everyone calls marriage one of life’s biggest steps, but hardly anyone talks about the questions that actually matter. Most pre-wedding conversations revolve around venues, guest lists, rituals, and who’s paying for what. Ironically, people gloss over the deeper stuff: the things that will shape years of daily living together. Do you both see the same kind of future? Can you weather disagreements without tearing each other down? Will money become a stress trigger? Are you free to be yourself in the relationship?
 Entrepreneur and content creator Ankur Warikoo has a way of cutting through all that surface chatter. In a candid LinkedIn post , he urged people to go beyond the usual checklist of “compatibility, love, and family approval”; to dig into your motivations, explore how you deal with conflict, talk about money upfront, preserve your sense of self, and speak honestly about the future you actually want.
 Honestly, this kind of advice clicks for many, especially in places like India where marriage often means the union of not just two individuals, but two entire families — complete with cultural baggage, expectations around careers and kids, and debates about where to live. Couples face a lot more than just learning to live together. Research backs up Warikoo’s point, as studies show that communication, shared expectations, and honesty about finances make a big difference. Organizations like the American Psychological Association stress the need for communication, while the Gottman Institute says to talk openly about everything from money to family plans.
 So what are these five crucial questions? And why do they matter so much?
 2 / 7 Why are you really getting married?
 First things first: is this what you want, or are you just caving under pressure? Are your parents nudging you, are friends settling down and making you feel left out, or is society telling you time is running out? Warikoo makes it clear: you have to separate your own wishes from everyone else’s expectations. Love, companionship, maybe even a sense of commitment can be good reasons. But if you’re acting out of fear or because you don’t want to disappoint family, you might regret it later.
 This is especially important in societies where family voices get loud. Respecting your parents matters, but in the end, it’s your life. Ask yourself honestly: are you comfortable with this person? Can you be yourself around them, without pretending or holding parts of you back? Most crucial of all: Are you choosing this relationship because you genuinely want it?
 3 / 7 How do you and your partner handle fights?
 Everyone gets into spats now and then. It’s not about whether you argue, but the how. When you disagree, do things get ugly? Is it insults, stonewalling, threats, or can you both sit down, listen, and try to find some middle ground?
 Per the American Psychological Association, the difference between a strong relationship and a fragile one often boils down to how you communicate when things are raw. Criticism, shouting, or emotional withdrawal damage trust and intimacy. Constructive conflict involves hearing each other out, staying respectful, owning your mistakes, and making up afterward.
 It’s easy to focus on chemistry and ease, but pay attention to moments when you don’t see eye to eye. Do you feel respected even when emotions run high? Building a long-term partnership means learning to disagree well.
 4 / 7 Are you financially aligned?
 Let’s be honest, money matters in marriage, and it’s rarely romantic. Warikoo suggests getting all the awkward questions out in the open: How will you split bills? Who manages what? What happens if someone loses a job or takes a break to support family? The American Psychological Association identifies money as a common source of relationship conflict. Working through debt, savings, spending habits, and whether you’ll help parents financially can head off years of resentment and misunderstanding.
 You don’t have to agree on every tiny detail, but you do need to know where the other person stands. Talk out your priorities and make space for differences, but don’t pretend money won’t play into your relationship. Honest conversations today make the hard moments easier down the road.
 5 / 7 Will you still have space to be yourself?
 A good marriage isn’t about dissolving into a single unit. It’s about building a life together while keeping your individuality. Warikoo throws this tough but necessary question out there: “Will you get to keep your friendships, hobbies, and ambitions? Or do you have to shrink yourself to fit a new mold?”
 A healthy marriage should let you grow as a person. That means finding time for your own interests, friendships, and dreams without constant guilt or pressure. You need to talk openly about your boundaries and how you’ll give each other real space, even as you tackle life as a team.
 6 / 7 Have you discussed the life you actually want?
 Love is powerful, but it doesn’t magically make your goals sync up. If you never talk about where you’ll live, what kind of daily rhythm you want, your career plans, whether to have kids, or what role extended family will play, resentment can quietly build.
 Warikoo isn’t interested in fairytale answers. He’s reminding you that sooner or later, you’ll need to work out how you’ll split chores, navigate careers, handle childcare, or care for aging parents. You don’t have to agree on everything, but you do need to know what matters most to each of you and say it out loud before you’re locked in.
 7 / 7 Why this all matters so much
 Saying yes to marriage should never be about just ticking off societal boxes or keeping up with other people’s timelines. All these questions aren’t there to “test” your compatibility, but to spark genuine, sometimes tough conversations about what marriage really offers, as well as demands, from you.
 A successful marriage isn’t about two people thinking exactly alike; it’s about building understanding, respect, and an ability to make decisions together, especially when life gets messy.
 So pause before saying yes. Ask yourself if you’re honestly ready for what comes the day after the wedding, when ordinary life sets in. Weddings are over in a day; the real partnership is built in all the little moments that come after.
